And now, as we eighteen men with our thirty-six arms, and one hundred and eighty thumbs and fingers, slowly toiled hour after hour upon that inert, sluggish corpse in the sea; and it seemed hardly to budge at all, except at long intervals; good evidence was hereby furnished of the enormousness of the mass we moved. For, upon the great canal of Hang-Ho, or whatever they call it, in China, four or five laborers on the foot-path will draw a bulky freighted junk at the rate of a mile an hour; but this grand argosy we towed heavily forged along, as if laden with pig-lead in bulk.

Darkness came on; but three lights up and down in the Pequod’s main-rigging dimly guided our way; till drawing nearer we saw Ahab dropping one of several more lanterns over the bulwarks. Vacantly eyeing the heaving whale for a moment, he issued the usual orders for securing it for the night, and then handing his lantern to a seaman, went his way into the cabin, and did not come forward again until morning.

Though, in overseeing the pursuit of this whale, Captain Ahab had evinced his customary activity, to call it so; yet now that the creature was dead, some vague dissatisfaction, or impatience, or despair, seemed working in him; as if the sight of that dead body reminded him that Moby Dick was yet to be slain; and though a thousand other whales were brought to his ship, all that would not one jot advance his grand, monomaniac object. Very soon you would have thought from the sound on the Pequod’s decks, that all hands were preparing to cast anchor in the deep; for heavy chains are being dragged along the deck, and thrust rattling out of the port-holes. But by those clanking links, the vast corpse itself, not the ship, is to be moored. Tied by the head to the stern, and by the tail to the bows, the whale now lies with its black hull close to the vessel’s and seen through the darkness of the night, which obscured the spars and rigging aloft, the two—ship and whale, seemed yoked together like colossal bullocks, whereof one reclines while the other remains standing.*

*A little item may as well be related here. The strongest and most reliable hold which the ship has upon the whale when moored alongside, is by the flukes or tail; and as from its greater density that part is relatively heavier than any other (excepting the side-fins), its flexibility even in death, causes it to sink low beneath the surface; so that with the hand you cannot get at it from the boat, in order to put the chain round it. But this difficulty is ingeniously overcome: a small, strong line is prepared with a wooden float at its outer end, and a weight in its middle, while the other end is secured to the ship. By adroit management the wooden float is made to rise on the other side of the mass, so that now having girdled the whale, the chain is readily made to follow suit; and being slipped along the body, is at last locked fast round the smallest part of the tail, at the point of junction with its broad flukes or lobes.

If moody Ahab was now all quiescence, at least so far as could be known on deck, Stubb, his second mate, flushed with conquest, betrayed an unusual but still good-natured excitement. Such an unwonted bustle was he in that the staid Starbuck, his official superior, quietly resigned to him for the time the sole management of affairs. One small, helping cause of all this liveliness in Stubb, was soon made strangely manifest. Stubb was a high liver; he was somewhat intemperately fond of the whale as a flavorish thing to his palate.
“A steak, a steak, ere I sleep! You, Daggoo! overboard you go, and cut me one from his small!”

Here be it known, that though these wild fishermen do not, as a general thing, and according to the great military maxim, make the enemy defray the current expenses of the war (at least before realizing the proceeds of the voyage), yet now and then you find some of these Nantucketers who have a genuine relish for that particular part of the Sperm Whale designated by Stubb; comprising the tapering extremity of the body.

About midnight that steak was cut and cooked; and lighted by two lanterns of sperm oil, Stubb stoutly stood up to his spermaceti supper at the capstan-head, as if that capstan were a sideboard. Nor was Stubb the only banqueter on whale’s flesh that night. Mingling their mumblings with his own mastications, thousands on thousands of sharks, swarming round the dead leviathan, smackingly feasted on its fatness. The few sleepers below in their bunks were often startled by the sharp slapping of their tails against the hull, within a few inches of the sleepers’ hearts. Peering over the side you could just see them (as before you heard them) wallowing in the sullen, black waters, and turning over on their backs as they scooped out huge globular pieces of the whale of the bigness of a human head. This particular feat of the shark seems all but miraculous. How at such an apparently unassailable surface, they contrive to gouge out such symmetrical mouthfuls, remains a part of the universal problem of all things. The mark they thus leave on the whale, may best be likened to the hollow made by a carpenter in countersinking for a screw.

Though amid all the smoking horror and diabolism of a sea-fight, sharks will be seen longingly gazing up to the ship’s decks, like hungry dogs round a table where red meat is being carved, ready to bolt down every killed man that is tossed to them; and though, while the valiant butchers over the deck-table are thus cannibally carving each other’s live meat with carving-knives all gilded and tasselled, the sharks, also, with their jewel-hilted mouths, are quarrelsomely carving away under the table at the dead meat; and though, were you to turn the whole affair upside down, it would still be pretty much the same thing, that is to say, a shocking sharkish business enough for all parties; and though sharks also are the invariable outriders of all slave ships crossing the Atlantic, systematically trotting alongside, to be handy in case a parcel is to be carried anywhere, or a dead slave to be decently buried; and though one or two other like instances might be set down, touching the set terms, places, and occasions, when sharks do most socially congregate, and most hilariously feast; yet is there no conceivable time or occasion when you will find them in such countless numbers, and in gayer or more jovial spirits, than around a dead sperm whale, moored by night to a whaleship at sea. If you have never seen that sight, then suspend your decision about the propriety of devil-worship, and the expediency of conciliating the devil.
But, as yet, Stubb heeded not the mumblings of the banquet that was going on so nigh him, no more than the sharks heeded the smacking of his own epicurean lips.

“Cook, cook!—where’s that old Fleece?” he cried at length, widening his legs still further, as if to form a more secure base for his supper; and, at the same time darting his fork into the dish, as if stabbing with his lance; “cook, you cook!—sail this way, cook!”

The old black, not in any very high glee at having been previously roused from his warm hammock at a most unseasonable hour, came shambling along from his galley, for, like many old blacks, there was something the matter with his knee-pans, which he did not keep well scoured like his other pans; this old Fleece, as they called him, came shuffling and limping along, assisting his step with his tongs, which, after a clumsy fashion, were made of straightened iron hoops; this old Ebony floundered along, and in obedience to the word of command, came to a dead stop on the opposite side of Stubb’s sideboard; when, with both hands folded before him, and resting on his two-legged cane, he bowed his arched back still further over, at the same time sideways inclining his head, so as to bring his best ear into play.

“Cook,” said Stubb, rapidly lifting a rather reddish morsel to his mouth, “don’t you think this steak is rather overdone? You’ve been beating this steak too much, cook; it’s too tender. Don’t I always say that to be good, a whale-steak must be tough? There are those sharks now over the side, don’t you see they prefer it tough and rare? What a shindy they are kicking up! Cook, go and talk to ’em; tell ’em they are welcome to help themselves civilly, and in moderation, but they must keep quiet. Blast me, if I can hear my own voice. Away, cook, and deliver my message. Here, take this lantern,” snatching one from his sideboard; “now then, go and preach to ’em!”

Sullenly taking the offered lantern, old Fleece limped across the deck to the bulwarks; and then, with one hand dropping his light low over the sea, so as to get a good view of his congregation, with the other hand he solemnly flourished his tongs, and leaning far over the side in a mumbling voice began addressing the sharks, while Stubb, softly crawling behind, overheard all that was said.

“Fellow-critters: I’se ordered here to say dat you must stop dat dam noise dare. You hear? Stop dat dam smackin’ ob de lip! Massa Stubb say dat you can fill your dam bellies up to de hatchings, but by Gor! you must stop dat dam racket!”

“Cook,” here interposed Stubb, accompanying the word with a sudden slap on the shoulder,—“Cook! why, damn your eyes, you mustn’t swear that way when you’re preaching. That’s no way to convert sinners, cook!”
“Who dat? Den preach to him yourself,” sullenly turning to go.
“No, cook; go on, go on.”
“Well, den, Belubed fellow-critters:”—
“Right!” exclaimed Stubb, approvingly, “coax ’em to it; try that,” and Fleece continued.

“Do you is all sharks, and by natur wery woracious, yet I zay to you, fellow-critters, dat dat woraciousness—’top dat dam slappin’ ob de tail! How you tink to hear, spose you keep up such a dam slappin’ and bitin’ dare?”
“Cook,” cried Stubb, collaring him, “I won’t have that swearing. Talk to ’em gentlemanly.”
Once more the sermon proceeded.

“Your woraciousness, fellow-critters, I don’t blame ye so much for; dat is natur, and can’t be helped; but to gobern dat wicked natur, dat is de pint. You is sharks, sartin; but if you gobern de shark in you, why den you be angel; for all angel is not’ing more dan de shark well goberned. Now, look here, bred’ren, just try wonst to be cibil, a helping yourselbs from dat whale. Don’t be tearin’ de blubber out your neighbour’s mout, I say. Is not one shark dood right as toder to dat whale? And, by Gor, none on you has de right to dat whale; dat whale belong to some one else. I know some o’ you has berry brig mout, brigger dan oders; but den de brig mouts sometimes has de small bellies; so dat de brigness of de mout is not to swaller wid, but to bit off de blubber for de small fry ob sharks, dat can’t get into de scrouge to help demselves.”
“Well done, old Fleece!” cried Stubb, “that’s Christianity; go on.”

“No use goin’ on; de dam willains will keep a scougin’ and slappin’ each oder, Massa Stubb; dey don’t hear one word; no use a-preachin’ to such dam g’uttons as you call ’em, till dare bellies is full, and dare bellies is bottomless; and when dey do get ’em full, dey wont hear you den; for den dey sink in de sea, go fast to sleep on de coral, and can’t hear not’ing at all, no more, for eber and eber.”
“Upon my soul, I am about of the same opinion; so give the benediction, Fleece, and I’ll away to my supper.”
Upon this, Fleece, holding both hands over the fishy mob, raised his shrill voice, and cried—
“Cussed fellow-critters! Kick up de damndest row as ever you can; fill your dam’ bellies ’till dey bust—and den die.”
“Now, cook,” said Stubb, resuming his supper at the capstan; “stand just where you stood before, there, over against me, and pay particular attention.”
“All dention,” said Fleece, again stooping over upon his tongs in the desired position.
“Well,” said Stubb, helping himself freely meanwhile; “I shall now go back to the subject of this steak. In the first place, how old are you, cook?”
“What dat do wid de ’teak,” said the old black, testily.
“Silence! How old are you, cook?”
“’Bout ninety, dey say,” he gloomily muttered.

“And you have lived in this world hard upon one hundred years, cook, and don’t know yet how to cook a whale-steak?” rapidly bolting another mouthful at the last word, so that morsel seemed a continuation of the question. “Where were you born, cook?”
“’Hind de hatchway, in ferry-boat, goin’ ober de Roanoke.”
“Born in a ferry-boat! That’s queer, too. But I want to know what country you were born in, cook!”
“Didn’t I say de Roanoke country?” he cried sharply.
“No, you didn’t, cook; but I’ll tell you what I’m coming to, cook. You must go home and be born over again; you don’t know how to cook a whale-steak yet.”
“Bress my soul, if I cook noder one,” he growled, angrily, turning round to depart.

“Come back, cook;—here, hand me those tongs;—now take that bit of steak there, and tell me if you think that steak cooked as it should be? Take it, I say”—holding the tongs towards him—“take it, and taste it.”
Faintly smacking his withered lips over it for a moment, the old negro muttered, “Best cooked ’teak I eber taste; joosy, berry joosy.”
“Cook,” said Stubb, squaring himself once more; “do you belong to the church?”
“Passed one once in Cape-Down,” said the old man sullenly.

“And you have once in your life passed a holy church in Cape-Town, where you doubtless overheard a holy parson addressing his hearers as his beloved fellow-creatures, have you, cook! And yet you come here, and tell me such a dreadful lie as you did just now, eh?” said Stubb. “Where do you expect to go to, cook?”
“Go to bed berry soon,” he mumbled, half-turning as he spoke.
“Avast! heave to! I mean when you die, cook. It’s an awful question. Now what’s your answer?”
“When dis old brack man dies,” said the negro slowly, changing his whole air and demeanor, “he hisself won’t go nowhere; but some bressed angel will come and fetch him.”
“Fetch him? How? In a coach and four, as they fetched Elijah? And fetch him where?”
“Up dere,” said Fleece, holding his tongs straight over his head, and keeping it there very solemnly.
“So, then, you expect to go up into our main-top, do you, cook, when you are dead? But don’t you know the higher you climb, the colder it gets? Main-top, eh?”
“Didn’t say dat t’all,” said Fleece, again in the sulks.

“You said up there, didn’t you? and now look yourself, and see where your tongs are pointing. But, perhaps you expect to get into heaven by crawling through the lubber’s hole, cook; but, no, no, cook, you don’t get there, except you go the regular way, round by the rigging. It’s a ticklish business, but must be done, or else it’s no go. But none of us are in heaven yet. Drop your tongs, cook, and hear my orders. Do ye hear? Hold your hat in one hand, and clap t’other a’top of your heart, when I’m giving my orders, cook. What! that your heart, there?—that’s your gizzard! Aloft! aloft!—that’s it—now you have it. Hold it there now, and pay attention.”
“All ’dention,” said the old black, with both hands placed as desired, vainly wriggling his grizzled head, as if to get both ears in front at one and the same time.

“Well then, cook, you see this whale-steak of yours was so very bad, that I have put it out of sight as soon as possible; you see that, don’t you? Well, for the future, when you cook another whale-steak for my private table here, the capstan, I’ll tell you what to do so as not to spoil it by overdoing. Hold the steak in one hand, and show a live coal to it with the other; that done, dish it; d’ye hear? And now to-morrow, cook, when we are cutting in the fish, be sure you stand by to get the tips of his fins; have them put in pickle. As for the ends of the flukes, have them soused, cook. There, now ye may go.”
But Fleece had hardly got three paces off, when he was recalled.

“Cook, give me cutlets for supper to-morrow night in the mid-watch. D’ye hear? away you sail, then.—Halloa! stop! make a bow before you go.—Avast heaving again! Whale-balls for breakfast—don’t forget.”

“Wish, by gor! whale eat him, ’stead of him eat whale. I’m bressed if he ain’t more of shark dan Massa Shark hisself,” muttered the old man, limping away; with which sage ejaculation he went to his hammock.

“And you have once in your life passed a holy church in Cape-Town, where you doubtless overheard a holy parson addressing his hearers as his beloved fellow-creatures, have you, cook! And yet you come here, and tell me such a dreadful lie as you did just now, eh?” said Stubb. “Where do you expect to go to, cook?”
“Go to bed berry soon,” he mumbled, half-turning as he spoke.
“Avast! heave to! I mean when you die, cook. It’s an awful question. Now what’s your answer?”
“When dis old brack man dies,” said the negro slowly, changing his whole air and demeanor, “he hisself won’t go nowhere; but some bressed angel will come and fetch him.”
“Fetch him? How? In a coach and four, as they fetched Elijah? And fetch him where?”
“Up dere,” said Fleece, holding his tongs straight over his head, and keeping it there very solemnly.
“So, then, you expect to go up into our main-top, do you, cook, when you are dead? But don’t you know the higher you climb, the colder it gets? Main-top, eh?”
“Didn’t say dat t’all,” said Fleece, again in the sulks.

“You said up there, didn’t you? and now look yourself, and see where your tongs are pointing. But, perhaps you expect to get into heaven by crawling through the lubber’s hole, cook; but, no, no, cook, you don’t get there, except you go the regular way, round by the rigging. It’s a ticklish business, but must be done, or else it’s no go. But none of us are in heaven yet. Drop your tongs, cook, and hear my orders. Do ye hear? Hold your hat in one hand, and clap t’other a’top of your heart, when I’m giving my orders, cook. What! that your heart, there?—that’s your gizzard! Aloft! aloft!—that’s it—now you have it. Hold it there now, and pay attention.”
“All ’dention,” said the old black, with both hands placed as desired, vainly wriggling his grizzled head, as if to get both ears in front at one and the same time.

“Well then, cook, you see this whale-steak of yours was so very bad, that I have put it out of sight as soon as possible; you see that, don’t you? Well, for the future, when you cook another whale-steak for my private table here, the capstan, I’ll tell you what to do so as not to spoil it by overdoing. Hold the steak in one hand, and show a live coal to it with the other; that done, dish it; d’ye hear? And now to-morrow, cook, when we are cutting in the fish, be sure you stand by to get the tips of his fins; have them put in pickle. As for the ends of the flukes, have them soused, cook. There, now ye may go.”
But Fleece had hardly got three paces off, when he was recalled.

“Cook, give me cutlets for supper to-morrow night in the mid-watch. D’ye hear? away you sail, then.—Halloa! stop! make a bow before you go.—Avast heaving again! Whale-balls for breakfast—don’t forget.”

“Wish, by gor! whale eat him, ’stead of him eat whale. I’m bressed if he ain’t more of shark dan Massa Shark hisself,” muttered the old man, limping away; with which sage ejaculation he went to his hammock.

modern_en.title: Chapter 64 — Stubb’s Supper
paragraphs: Stubb's whale had been killed some way off from the ship. There was a dead calm, so we formed a tandem of three boats and began the slow job of towing the trophy back to the Pequod. Hour after hour we eighteen men, with our thirty-six arms and one hundred and eighty thumbs and fingers, labored at that inert, sluggish corpse in the sea, and it seemed hardly to budge at all except at long intervals — plenty of proof of how enormous a mass we were moving. On the great canal of Hang-Ho, or whatever they call it, in China, four or five laborers on the towpath can haul a bulky loaded junk at a mile an hour; but this grand argosy of ours forged heavily along as if its hold were packed with pig-lead.

Darkness fell, but three lights hung up and down the Pequod's main-rigging dimly showed us the way; and as we drew nearer we saw Ahab lowering one of several more lanterns over the bulwarks. He looked blankly at the heaving whale for a moment, gave the usual orders for making it fast for the night, and then handed his lantern to a seaman and went off into the cabin, not coming forward again until morning.

Captain Ahab had shown his usual activity, if you can call it that, in directing the chase of this whale; but now that the creature was dead, some vague dissatisfaction, impatience, or despair seemed to be at work in him — as if the sight of that dead body reminded him that Moby Dick was still to be killed, and that even if a thousand other whales were brought to his ship, not one of them would bring his grand, monomaniac goal one jot closer. Soon, from the noise on the Pequod's decks, you would have thought all hands were getting ready to drop anchor in the deep; heavy chains are being dragged along the deck and shoved rattling out through the portholes. But those clanking links are meant to moor not the ship but the vast corpse itself. Tied by the head to the stern and by the tail to the bows, the whale now lies with its black hull close against the vessel's; and seen through the dark of night, which hid the spars and rigging overhead, the two — ship and whale — looked yoked together like colossal bullocks, one lying down while the other stands.*

*A little item may as well be told here. The strongest and most reliable hold the ship has on the whale when moored alongside is by the flukes, or tail; and since that part, from its greater density, is relatively heavier than any other (except the side-fins), its flexibility, even in death, makes it sink low beneath the surface, so that you cannot reach it by hand from the boat to put the chain around it. But this difficulty is ingeniously overcome: a small, strong line is prepared with a wooden float at its outer end and a weight in its middle, while the other end is made fast to the ship. By skillful management the wooden float is made to rise on the other side of the mass, so that, the line having now girdled the whale, the chain is easily made to follow; and being slipped along the body, it is at last locked fast around the smallest part of the tail, where it joins the broad flukes or lobes.

If moody Ahab was now all stillness, at least as far as could be known on deck, Stubb, his second mate, flushed with conquest, showed an unusual but still good-natured excitement. He was in such an unaccustomed bustle that the sober Starbuck, his official superior, quietly left the sole management of affairs to him for the time being. One small contributing cause of all this liveliness in Stubb was soon made strangely plain. Stubb was a high liver; he was somewhat intemperately fond of the whale as a thing flavorful to his palate.
"A steak, a steak, before I sleep! You, Daggoo! Overboard you go, and cut me one from his small!"

It should be known here that although these wild fishermen do not, as a general rule, follow the great military maxim of making the enemy pay the running expenses of the war (at least not before realizing the proceeds of the voyage), yet now and then you find some of these Nantucketers who have a genuine relish for that particular part of the Sperm Whale that Stubb named, which takes in the tapering end of the body.

Around midnight the steak was cut and cooked, and by the light of two sperm-oil lanterns Stubb stood up stoutly to his spermaceti supper at the capstan-head, as though the capstan were a sideboard. Nor was Stubb the only one feasting on whale meat that night. Thousands upon thousands of sharks, swarming around the dead leviathan, mixed their mumblings with his chewing as they feasted noisily on its fat. The few sleepers in their bunks below were often startled by the sharp slap of the sharks' tails against the hull, only a few inches from their hearts. If you peered over the side you could just make them out (having heard them first), wallowing in the sullen black water and rolling onto their backs as they scooped huge round chunks the size of a human head out of the whale. This particular feat of the shark seems almost miraculous. How they manage to gouge such symmetrical mouthfuls out of a surface that looks impossible to bite into remains part of the universal problem of all things. The mark they leave on the whale is best compared to the hollow a carpenter makes when countersinking for a screw.

Amid all the smoking horror and devilry of a sea-fight, sharks can be seen gazing longingly up at the ship's decks, like hungry dogs around a table where red meat is being carved, ready to gulp down every dead man thrown to them. While the valiant butchers at the deck-table are cannibally carving one another's live flesh with gilded, tasseled carving-knives, the sharks, with their jewel-hilted mouths, are carving away quarrelsomely under the table at the dead meat — and if you turned the whole affair upside down it would still be much the same thing, that is, a shocking, sharkish business all round. Sharks are also the unfailing outriders of every slave ship crossing the Atlantic, trotting methodically alongside, handy in case a parcel needs carrying somewhere or a dead slave needs a decent burial. And one or two other such cases could be listed, concerning the set times, places, and occasions when sharks gather most sociably and feast most hilariously. Yet there is no conceivable time or occasion when you will find them in such countless numbers, or in gayer and more jovial spirits, than around a dead sperm whale moored at night to a whaleship at sea. If you have never seen that sight, then hold off deciding whether devil-worship is proper and whether it is wise to keep on the good side of the devil.
But as yet Stubb paid no attention to the mumblings of the banquet going on so close to him, any more than the sharks noticed the smacking of his own gourmet lips.

"Cook, cook! — where's that old Fleece?" he cried at length, spreading his legs still wider as if to form a more secure base for his supper, and at the same time stabbing his fork into the dish as if it were a lance. "Cook, you cook! — sail this way, cook!"

The old black, in no great glee at having already been roused from his warm hammock at a most unseasonable hour, came shambling out of his galley. Like many old blacks, he had something wrong with his knee-pans, which he did not keep as well scoured as his other pans. This old Fleece, as they called him, came shuffling and limping along, propping up his step with his tongs, a clumsy pair made of straightened iron hoops. This old Ebony floundered forward and, as ordered, stopped dead on the far side of Stubb's sideboard. Then, with both hands folded in front of him and resting on his two-legged cane, he bent his arched back over still further, tilting his head to one side at the same time so as to bring his better ear into play.

"Cook," said Stubb, quickly lifting a rather reddish morsel to his mouth, "don't you think this steak is rather overdone? You've been beating this steak too much, cook; it's too tender. Don't I always say that to be good, a whale steak must be tough? There are those sharks now over the side — don't you see they prefer it tough and rare? What a racket they're kicking up! Cook, go and talk to them; tell them they are welcome to help themselves civilly, and in moderation, but they must keep quiet. Blast me if I can hear my own voice. Away, cook, and deliver my message. Here, take this lantern," snatching one from his sideboard; "now then, go and preach to them!"

Sullenly, old Fleece took the lantern he was offered and limped across the deck to the bulwarks. Then, holding his light low over the sea with one hand to get a good look at his congregation, he solemnly waved his tongs with the other, leaned far out over the side, and began to address the sharks in a mumbling voice, while Stubb crept softly up behind him and overheard everything that was said.

"Fellow-critters: I'se ordered here to say dat you must stop dat damn noise dere. You hear? Stop dat damn smackin' of de lip! Massa Stubb say dat you can fill your damn bellies up to de hatches, but by Gor! you must stop dat damn racket!"
"Cook," Stubb cut in here, with a sudden slap on the shoulder, "Cook! Why, damn your eyes, you mustn't swear that way when you're preaching. That's no way to convert sinners, cook!"
"Who dat? Den preach to him yourself," sullenly turning to go.
"No, cook. Go on, go on."
"Well, den, beloved fellow-critters:" —
"Right!" exclaimed Stubb approvingly. "Coax them into it. Try that." And Fleece continued.

"Though you is all sharks, and by natur' very voracious, yet I say to you, fellow-critters, dat dat voraciousness — 'top dat damn slappin' of de tail! How you tink to hear, s'pose you keep up such a damn slappin' and bitin' dere?"
"Cook," cried Stubb, grabbing him by the collar, "I won't have that swearing. Talk to them like a gentleman."
Once more the sermon proceeded.

"Your voraciousness, fellow-critters, I don't blame you so much for; dat is natur', and can't be helped; but to govern dat wicked natur', dat is de point. You is sharks, certain; but if you govern de shark in you, why den you be angel; for all angel is nothin' more dan de shark well governed. Now, look here, brethren, just try once to be civil, a-helpin' yourselves from dat whale. Don't be tearin' de blubber out of your neighbor's mouth, I say. Ain't one shark got as good a right as de other to dat whale? And, by Gor, none of you has de right to dat whale; dat whale belong to somebody else. I know some of you has very big mouth, bigger dan others; but den de big mouths sometimes has de small bellies; so dat de bigness of de mouth is not to swallow wid, but to bite off de blubber for de small fry of sharks, dat can't get into de crush to help demselves."
"Well done, old Fleece!" cried Stubb. "That's Christianity. Go on."

"No use goin' on; de damn villains will keep a-jostlin' and slappin' each other, Massa Stubb; dey don't hear one word; no use a-preachin' to such damn gluttons as you call 'em, till dere bellies is full, and dere bellies is bottomless; and when dey do get 'em full, dey won't hear you den; for den dey sink in de sea, go fast to sleep on de coral, and can't hear nothin' at all, no more, for ever and ever."
"Upon my soul, I am about of the same opinion. So give the benediction, Fleece, and I'll get back to my supper."
Upon this, Fleece, holding both hands over the fishy mob, raised his shrill voice and cried —
"Cussed fellow-critters! Kick up de damnedest row as ever you can; fill your damn bellies till dey bust — and den die."
"Now, cook," said Stubb, resuming his supper at the capstan, "stand just where you stood before, there, across from me, and pay particular attention."
"All 'tention," said Fleece, again stooping over his tongs in the desired position.
"Well," said Stubb, helping himself generously meanwhile, "I shall now go back to the subject of this steak. In the first place, how old are you, cook?"
"What dat do wid de steak?" said the old black, testily.
"Silence! How old are you, cook?"
"'Bout ninety, dey say," he muttered gloomily.

"And you have lived in this world close to one hundred years, cook, and don't know yet how to cook a whale steak?" — rapidly swallowing another mouthful at the last word, so that it seemed a continuation of the question. "Where were you born, cook?"
"'Hind de hatchway, in ferry-boat, goin' over de Roanoke."
"Born on a ferryboat! That's odd, too. But I want to know what country you were born in, cook!"
"Didn't I say de Roanoke country?" he cried sharply.
"No, you didn't, cook. But I'll tell you what I'm getting at, cook. You must go home and be born all over again. You don't know how to cook a whale steak yet."
"Bress my soul if I cook anoder one," he growled angrily, turning around to leave.

"Come back, cook — here, hand me those tongs — now take that bit of steak there, and tell me if you think that steak is cooked as it should be? Take it, I say" — holding the tongs toward him — "take it, and taste it."
Faintly smacking his withered lips over it for a moment, the old negro muttered, "Best cooked steak I ever taste; joosy, very joosy."
"Cook," said Stubb, squaring himself once more, "do you belong to the church?"
"Passed one once in Cape-Down," said the old man sullenly.

"And you have once in your life passed a holy church in Cape Town, where you no doubt overheard a holy parson addressing his listeners as his beloved fellow-creatures — have you, cook! And yet you come here and tell me such a dreadful lie as you just did, eh?" said Stubb. "Where do you expect to go, cook?"
"Go to bed very soon," he mumbled, half-turning as he spoke.
"Halt! Heave to! I mean when you die, cook. It's an awful question. Now what's your answer?"
"When dis old black man dies," said the negro slowly, changing his whole air and manner, "he hisself won't go nowhere; but some bressed angel will come and fetch him."
"Fetch him? How? In a coach and four, as they fetched Elijah? And fetch him where?"
"Up dere," said Fleece, holding his tongs straight over his head and keeping them there very solemnly.
"So you expect to go up to our main-top when you die, do you, cook? But don't you know that the higher you climb, the colder it gets? The main-top, eh?"
"Didn't say dat at all," said Fleece, sulking again.

"You said up there, didn't you? And now look for yourself and see where your tongs are pointing. But perhaps you expect to get into heaven by crawling through the lubber's hole (the opening through a mast's top platform that novice climbers use), cook; but no, no, cook, you don't get there unless you go the regular way, round by the rigging. It's a ticklish business, but it must be done, or else it's no go. But none of us are in heaven yet. Drop your tongs, cook, and hear my orders. Do you hear? Hold your hat in one hand, and clap the other on top of your heart when I'm giving my orders, cook. What! That your heart, there? — that's your gizzard! Aloft! Aloft! — that's it — now you have it. Hold it there now, and pay attention."
"All 'tention," said the old black, placing both hands as requested, vainly wriggling his grizzled head as if trying to get both ears in front at one and the same time.

"Well then, cook, you see, this whale steak of yours was so very bad that I've put it out of sight as fast as I could; you see that, don't you? Well, from now on, when you cook another whale steak for my private table here, the capstan, I'll tell you what to do so you don't spoil it by overcooking. Hold the steak in one hand and show a live coal to it with the other; once that's done, serve it up. Hear me? And tomorrow, cook, when we're cutting in the fish, make sure you're standing by to get the tips of his fins; have them pickled. As for the ends of the flukes, have them soused, cook. There, now you can go."
But Fleece had hardly gotten three steps away when he was called back.
"Cook, give me cutlets for supper tomorrow night during the mid-watch. Do you hear? Away you sail, then. — Wait! Stop! Make a bow before you go. — Hold on! Whale-balls for breakfast — don't forget."

"Wish, by Gor, whale eat him, 'stead of him eat whale. I'm bressed if he ain't more of shark dan Massa Shark hisself," muttered the old man, limping away; and with this sage outburst he went to his hammock.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 64 — Stubbs aftensmad
paragraphs: Stubbs hval var blevet dræbt et stykke fra skibet. Der var blikstille, så vi dannede en række af tre både efter hinanden og tog fat på det langsomme arbejde med at slæbe trofæet tilbage til Pequod. Time efter time sled vi atten mand med vores seksogtredive arme og hundrede og firs tommelfingre og fingre med det livløse, trægt lig i havet, og det syntes næsten ikke at røre sig, undtagen med lange mellemrum — rigeligt bevis på, hvor enorm en masse vi flyttede. På den store Hang-Ho-kanal, eller hvad de nu kalder den, i Kina kan fire eller fem arbejdere på slæbestien hale en tung lastet junke af sted med en engelsk mil i timen; men vores stolte lastskib sejlede tungt frem, som om dens lastrum var pakket med blybarrer.

Mørket faldt på, men tre lygter, der hang op og ned i Pequods stor-rigning, viste os svagt vejen; og da vi kom nærmere, så vi Ahab sænke en af flere andre lanterner ned over rælingen. Han så et øjeblik tomt på den duvende hval, gav de sædvanlige ordrer til at gøre den fast for natten, rakte så sin lanterne til en sømand og gik ind i kahytten, uden at komme frem igen før om morgenen.

Kaptajn Ahab havde vist sin sædvanlige virksomhed, hvis man kan kalde det det, under ledelsen af jagten på denne hval; men nu, da dyret var dødt, syntes en vag utilfredshed, utålmodighed eller fortvivlelse at arbejde i ham — som om synet af det døde legeme mindede ham om, at Moby Dick stadig skulle dræbes, og at selv om tusind andre hvaler blev bragt til hans skib, ville ikke en eneste af dem bringe hans store, monomane mål en tøddel nærmere. Snart kunne man af larmen på Pequods dæk have troet, at alle mand gjorde klar til at kaste anker i dybet; tunge kæder slæbes hen ad dækket og skubbes raslende ud gennem portene. Men de klirrende led er beregnet til at fortøje ikke skibet, men selve det vældige lig. Bundet ved hovedet til agterstavnen og ved halen til forstavnen ligger hvalen nu med sit sorte skrog tæt op ad skibets; og set gennem nattens mørke, som skjulte rær og rigning højt oppe, så de to — skib og hval — ud som kolossale okser spændt sammen i åg, hvoraf den ene ligger ned, mens den anden står.*

*En lille detalje kan lige så godt fortælles her. Skibets stærkeste og mest pålidelige tag i hvalen, når den ligger fortøjet langs siden, er i halefinnerne, altså halen. Den del er på grund af sin større tæthed forholdsvis tungere end alle andre (undtagen brystfinnerne), og dens bøjelighed, selv i døden, får den til at synke dybt under overfladen. Man kan derfor ikke nå den med hånden fra båden for at lægge kæden om den. Men denne vanskelighed overvindes snildt. Man gør en lille, stærk line klar med en træflyder yderst og en vægt midt på, mens den anden ende gøres fast på skibet. Med dygtig håndtering får man træflyderen til at dukke op på den anden side af kroppen. Så har linen lagt sig som et bælte om hvalen, og kæden er let at få til at følge efter. Kæden glider langs kroppen og låses til sidst fast om halens smalleste del, der hvor den går over i de brede halefinner, eller lapper.

Hvis den tungsindige Ahab nu var helt stille, i hvert fald så vidt man kunne se på dækket, så viste Stubb, hans anden styrmand, der var høj af sejr, en usædvanlig, men stadig godmodig opstemthed. Han var i så uvant travlhed, at den nøgterne Starbuck, hans foresatte, stille overlod ham den fulde ledelse af arbejdet for en tid. En lille medvirkende grund til al denne livlighed hos Stubb blev snart underligt tydelig. Stubb levede højt. Han var lidt umådeholdent glad for hvalkød som noget, der smagte godt på hans gane.
»En bøf, en bøf, før jeg sover! Du, Daggoo! Over bord med dig, og skær mig en fra hans smalle!«

Det må nævnes her, at selv om disse vilde fiskere som regel ikke følger den store militære leveregel om at lade fjenden betale krigens løbende udgifter (i hvert fald ikke før de har fået udbyttet af rejsen hjem), så finder man nu og da nogle af disse nantucketere, der oprigtigt sætter pris på netop den del af kaskelotten, som Stubb nævnte, og som omfatter kroppens smalnende ende.

Omkring midnat var bøffen skåret og stegt, og i skæret fra to lanterner med kaskelotolie stod Stubb tappert og spiste sin hvalratsmiddag ved ankerspillets top, som om ankerspillet var et anretterbord. Stubb var heller ikke den eneste, der holdt festmåltid på hvalkød den nat. Tusinder og atter tusinder af hajer myldrede rundt om det døde havuhyre og blandede deres mumlen med hans tyggen, mens de fråssede støjende i dets spæk. De få sovende i køjerne nedenunder blev ofte skræmt op af hajernes skarpe halesmæk mod skroget, kun få tommer fra deres hjerter. Hvis man kikkede ud over rælingen, kunne man lige akkurat skimte dem (efter først at have hørt dem), mens de vælede rundt i det mutte sorte vand og rullede om på ryggen, når de skar store runde stykker, store som et menneskehoved, ud af hvalen. Hajernes kunststykke her virker næsten som et mirakel. Hvordan de bærer sig ad med at udhule så regelmæssige mundfulde af en overflade, der ser umulig ud at bide i, er stadig en del af alle tings almindelige gåde. Det mærke, de efterlader på hvalen, kan bedst sammenlignes med hullet, en tømrer laver, når han forsænker en skrue.

Midt i al skrækken og djævelskabet fra et søslag kan man se hajer kigge længselsfuldt op mod skibets dæk som sultne hunde rundt om et bord, hvor der skæres rødt kød, parate til at sluge hver eneste døde mand, der bliver kastet til dem. Mens de tapre slagtere ved dæksbordet kannibalsk skærer i hinandens levende kød med forgyldte, kvastprydede forskærerknive, skærer hajerne med deres juvelbesatte kæfter kævlende løs under bordet i det døde kød. Og vendte man hele sagen på hovedet, ville det stadig være omtrent det samme, nemlig en chokerende, hajagtig affære hele vejen rundt. Hajer er også de ufejlbarlige ledsagere af ethvert slaveskib, der krydser Atlanten. De trasker metodisk ved siden af, parat hvis en pakke skal bæres et sted hen, eller en død slave skal have en anstændig begravelse. Og et par andre sådanne tilfælde kunne nævnes, om de faste tider, steder og lejligheder, hvor hajer samles mest selskabeligt og fester mest lystigt. Men der er ingen tænkelig tid eller lejlighed, hvor man finder dem i så utallige mængder eller i et gladere og mere muntert humør end rundt om en død kaskelot, der om natten ligger fortøjet ved et hvalfangerskib på havet. Hvis du aldrig har set det syn, så vent med at afgøre, om djævelsdyrkelse er det rette, og om det er klogt at holde sig på god fod med djævelen.
Men indtil videre var Stubb ligeglad med mumlen fra banketten, der foregik så tæt på ham, lige så lidt som hajerne lagde mærke til smasken fra hans egne fine læber.

»Kok, kok! — hvor er den gamle Fleece?« råbte han til sidst og stillede benene endnu bredere, som for at få et sikrere fundament til sin middag, og stak samtidig gaflen i retten, som var den en lanse. »Kok, din kok! — sejl herhen, kok!«

Den gamle sorte mand var langt fra glad for allerede at være blevet vækket af sin varme hængekøje på et højst upassende tidspunkt. Han kom subbende ud af sit kabys. Som mange gamle sorte havde han noget galt med knæskallerne, som han ikke holdt så blankskurede som sine andre gryder og pander. Den gamle Fleece, som de kaldte ham, kom subbende og haltende frem og støttede sit skridt med sin ildtang, et klodset par af udrettede tøndebånd af jern. Den gamle Ibenholt famlede frem og standsede, som han var beordret til, brat på den anden side af Stubbs anretterbord. Så foldede han begge hænder foran sig, støttede dem på sin tobenede stok, bøjede sin krumme ryg endnu mere og lagde hovedet på skrå for at få sit bedste øre i brug.

»Kok,« sagde Stubb og løftede hurtigt en ret rødlig bid til munden, »synes du ikke, at denne bøf er lidt for gennemstegt? Du har banket for meget på den bøf, kok. Den er for mør. Siger jeg ikke altid, at en hvalbøf skal være sej for at være god? Se de hajer derovre ved siden af — kan du ikke se, at de foretrækker den sej og rå? Hvor de larmer! Kok, gå hen og tal med dem. Sig, at de er velkomne til at forsyne sig, høfligt og med måde, men at de skal være stille. Fanden æde mig, hvis jeg kan høre min egen stemme. Af sted, kok, og bring min besked. Her, tag den her lanterne,« og han snappede en fra anretterbordet. »Nu af sted, og prædik for dem!«

Surt tog den gamle Fleece den lanterne, han fik, og haltede hen over dækket til skansekledningen. Så holdt han lyset lavt ud over havet med den ene hånd for at få et godt kig på sin menighed, svingede højtideligt ildtangen med den anden, lænede sig langt ud over rælingen og begyndte at tale til hajerne med mumlende stemme. Stubb sneg sig imens stille op bag ham og overhørte alt, hvad der blev sagt.

»Medskabninger: Jeg er sat til at sige jer, at I skal holde det forbandede spektakel dér op. Hører I? Hold det forbandede smasken med læberne op! Massa Stubb siger, at I godt må fylde jeres forbandede maver helt op til lugerne, men ved gud, så skal I holde det forbandede halløj op!«
»Kok,« faldt Stubb ind og slog ham pludselig på skulderen, »kok! Forbandet være dine øjne, du må ikke bande sådan, når du prædiker. Det er ikke den måde at omvende syndere på, kok!«
»Hvem dér? Så præk selv for dem,« sagde han surt og vendte sig for at gå.
»Nej, kok. Fortsæt, fortsæt.«
»Nå, så, kære medskabninger:« —
»Rigtigt!« udbrød Stubb anerkendende. »Overtal dem pænt. Prøv det.« Og Fleece fortsatte.

»Skønt I alle er hajer og af natur meget grådige, så siger jeg til jer, medskabninger, at den grådighed — hold op med det forbandede smæk med halen! Hvordan tror I, I kan høre noget, hvis I bliver ved med at smække og bide dér?«
»Kok,« råbte Stubb og greb ham i kraven, »jeg vil ikke have, at du bander sådan. Tal til dem som en gentleman.«
Endnu en gang fortsatte prædikenen.

»Jeres grådighed, medskabninger, den bebrejder jeg jer ikke så meget; det er natur og kan ikke hjælpes. Men at styre den onde natur, det er pointen. I er hajer, vist nok, men hvis I styrer hajen i jer, ja, så er I engle. For alle engle er ikke andet end hajer, der er godt styret. Nu, se her, brødre, prøv bare én gang at være høflige, når I forsyner jer af den hval. Riv ikke spækket ud af munden på jeres nabo, siger jeg. Har ikke én haj lige så god ret som den anden til den hval? Og ved gud, ingen af jer har ret til den hval. Den hval tilhører en anden. Jeg ved, nogle af jer har meget store munde, større end andre. Men de store munde har somme tider små maver. Så den store mund er ikke til at sluge med, men til at bide spæk af til de små hajyngel, der ikke kan komme ind i trængslen og forsyne sig selv.«
»Godt gået, gamle Fleece!« råbte Stubb. »Det er kristendom. Fortsæt.«

»Nytter ikke at fortsætte. De forbandede slyngler bliver ved med at skubbe og smække efter hinanden, Massa Stubb. De hører ikke et ord. Det nytter ikke at prædike for sådanne forbandede frådsere, som De kalder dem, før deres maver er fyldt, og deres maver er bundløse. Og når de så får dem fyldt, vil de ikke høre efter dengang heller. For så synker de i havet, falder i dyb søvn på korallerne og kan ikke høre noget som helst mere, i al evighed.«
»På min sjæl, jeg er omtrent af samme mening. Så giv velsignelsen, Fleece, så går jeg tilbage til min middag.«
Derpå holdt Fleece begge hænder ud over den fiskelugtende flok, hævede sin skingre stemme og råbte —
»Forbandede medskabninger! Lav det forbandedeste halløj, I overhovedet kan. Fyld jeres forbandede maver, til de revner — og dø så.«
»Nu, kok,« sagde Stubb og tog sin middag op igen ved ankerspillet, »stil dig præcis, hvor du stod før, dér, lige over for mig, og vær særlig opmærksom.«
»Al opmærksomhed,« sagde Fleece og bøjede sig atter over sin ildtang i den ønskede stilling.
»Godt,« sagde Stubb og forsynede sig rigeligt imens, »nu vender jeg tilbage til emnet med denne bøf. For det første, hvor gammel er du, kok?«
»Hvad har det med bøffen at gøre?« sagde den gamle sorte gnavent.
»Tys! Hvor gammel er du, kok?«
»Omkring halvfems, siger de,« mumlede han dystert.

»Og du har levet i denne verden i næsten hundrede år, kok, og ved stadig ikke, hvordan man steger en hvalbøf?« — og ved det sidste ord slugte han hurtigt en mundfuld til, så det lød som en fortsættelse af spørgsmålet. »Hvor er du født, kok?«
»Bag lugen, i en færge, på vej over Roanoke.«
»Født på en færge! Det er også mærkeligt. Men jeg vil vide, i hvilket land du er født, kok!«
»Sagde jeg ikke Roanoke-egnen?« råbte han skarpt.
»Nej, det gjorde du ikke, kok. Men jeg skal sige dig, hvad jeg vil frem til, kok. Du må tage hjem og fødes helt forfra. Du ved stadig ikke, hvordan man steger en hvalbøf.«
»Gud velsigne min sjæl, hvis jeg steger en til,« knurrede han vredt og vendte sig om for at gå.

»Kom tilbage, kok — her, giv mig den ildtang — nu tag det stykke bøf dér og sig mig, om du synes, den bøf er stegt, som den skal være. Tag den, siger jeg,« og han holdt tangen hen mod ham, »tag den og smag på den.«
Efter et øjeblik at have smasket svagt med sine indtørrede læber over den mumlede den gamle sorte mand: »Bedst stegte bøf, jeg nogen sinde har smagt. Saftig, meget saftig.«
»Kok,« sagde Stubb og stillede sig atter bredbenet, »hører du til i kirken?«
»Gik forbi en en gang i Kapstad,« sagde den gamle mand gnavent.

»Og du er en gang i dit liv gået forbi en hellig kirke i Kapstad, hvor du uden tvivl hørte en hellig pastor tale til sine tilhørere som sine kære medskabninger — har du det, kok! Og alligevel kommer du her og fortæller mig en så rædsom løgn som den, du lige sagde, hva?« sagde Stubb. »Hvor regner du med at komme hen, kok?«
»Går i seng meget snart,« mumlede han og vendte sig halvt, mens han talte.
»Stands! Læg bi! Jeg mener, når du dør, kok. Det er et frygteligt spørgsmål. Nå, hvad er dit svar?«
»Når den her gamle sorte mand dør,« sagde den sorte mand langsomt og ændrede hele sin holdning og væremåde, »så går han ikke nogen steder selv, men en velsignet engel kommer og henter ham.«
»Henter ham? Hvordan? I en firspand, som da de hentede Elias? Og henter ham hvorhen?«
»Op dér,« sagde Fleece og holdt sin ildtang lige op over hovedet og blev ved med at holde den dér meget højtideligt.
»Så du regner med at komme op i vores stortop, når du dør, gør du, kok? Men ved du ikke, at jo højere man kommer op, desto koldere bliver det? Stortoppen, hva?«
»Sagde slet ikke det,« sagde Fleece og surmulede igen.

»Du sagde op dér, ikke? Og se nu selv efter, hvor din ildtang peger hen. Men måske regner du med at komme i himlen ved at kravle gennem landkrabbehullet (åbningen gennem platformen i mastetoppen, som uøvede klatrere bruger), kok. Men nej, nej, kok, du kommer ikke derhen, medmindre du går den almindelige vej, udenom i vanterne. Det er en kildrende sag, men den må gøres, ellers går det ikke. Men ingen af os er i himlen endnu. Slip din ildtang, kok, og hør mine ordrer. Hører du? Hold din hat i den ene hånd og slå den anden oven på dit hjerte, når jeg giver mine ordrer, kok. Hvad! Er det dit hjerte, dér? — det er din kråse! Op! Op! — sådan — nu har du den. Hold den dér nu, og pas godt på.«
»Al opmærksomhed,« sagde den gamle sorte og placerede begge hænder som bedt, mens han forgæves vrikkede med sit gråsprængte hoved, som om han prøvede at få begge ører foran på samme tid.

»Nå, kok, ser du, den hvalbøf af din var så elendig, at jeg skyndte mig at få den af syne, så hurtigt jeg kunne. Det kan du vel godt se? Så fra nu af, når du steger en ny hvalbøf til mit private bord her, gangspillet, skal jeg sige dig, hvad du skal gøre, så du ikke ødelægger den ved at stege den for meget. Hold bøffen i den ene hånd og vis den et levende stykke gløde med den anden. Når det er gjort, så server den. Forstår du? Og i morgen, kok, når vi skærer fisken op, så sørg for at stå klar og få fat i spidserne af hans finner. Dem skal du lægge i eddike. Og enderne af halefinnen skal du lægge i lage, kok. Sådan, nu kan du gå.«
Men Fleece var knap kommet tre skridt væk, før han blev kaldt tilbage.

»Kok, jeg vil have koteletter til aftensmad i morgen nat under midtvagten. Hører du? Så sejl af sted med dig. — Vent! Stop! Buk dig, før du går. — Bliv stående! Hvalboller til morgenmad — glem det ikke.«

»Ønske, ved Gud, hval æde ham i stedet for han æde hval. Jeg blive velsignet, hvis han ikke mere haj end Massa Haj selv,« mumlede den gamle mand, mens han haltede af sted, og med dette kloge udbrud gik han i sin hængekøje.
